# GPU and Inference Systems Fundamentals

[← NVIDIA](../README.md) · [Every NVIDIA question](../../nvidia.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/gpu-and-inference-systems-fundamentals)

`gpu` `inference` `kernel` `matmul` `transformer`

---

## Requirements

Common areas include:

- Amdahl's Law and the constraints it places on speedup.
- The GPU memory hierarchy: registers, shared memory / SRAM, HBM, and global memory.
- High-level thread and block limits, plus why occupancy is significant.
- Matrix-multiplication complexity and tiling strategies.
- How matmul runs on CPUs versus GPUs.
- MLP tensor shapes, bias broadcasting, and framework-level operations.
- C++ basics: virtual methods, inline methods, and inheritance.
- Transformer QKV, and the difference between attention and RNN recurrence.
- Tensor parallelism compared with pipeline parallelism.
- Inference benchmarking measures: latency, throughput, p95 / p99, tokens/sec, and time-to-first-token.
- JAX versus PyTorch, including compiler-directed execution.
- The path from a frontend model definition to ONNX / a computation graph and then to GPU code / compiled kernels.

## Notes

Strong responses tie equations to the hardware.

- Multiplying an `M x K` matrix by a `K x N` matrix requires O(MKN) work; GPU performance improvements come from tiling, reusing data, and reducing expensive global-memory movement.
- Shared memory / SRAM offers much lower latency than HBM but has less capacity; tiling places submatrices nearer to the compute units.
- Under Amdahl's Law, when fraction `p` receives acceleration by speedup `s`, the overall speedup is `1 / ((1-p) + p/s)`.
- Tensor parallelism distributes operators / tensor dimensions among devices, whereas pipeline parallelism divides model layers into stages and passes microbatches through those stages.
- Inference benchmarks need to identify the workload shape: model, batch size, sequence length, prompt/output tokens, hardware, precision, and serving stack.

## Preparation

- Work out tiled-matmul memory reuse on a whiteboard.
- Have a brief comparison ready for PyTorch eager execution and JAX JIT / XLA compilation.
- Be prepared to cover NVIDIA Dynamo / Triton-style inference serving at a high level, including distributed serving, dynamic worker allocation, and latency / throughput trade-offs.
